tagline: A wise man's honest search for what lasts in a world where everything passes like a breath, framed by a teacher who points the reader back to the fear of God.
overview:
Ecclesiastes is the record of a search. A speaker who calls himself the Teacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth) sets out to find what a person actually gains from all the labor of a life lived under the sun. He tests pleasure, building, wealth, wisdom, and work. He watches the seasons turn, the powerful oppress the weak, the righteous die young, and the wicked die honored. Over all of it he sets one word, hevel, which the Berean Standard Bible translates as futility: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” (1:2).

Yet the book is not simply gloomy. Again and again the Teacher breaks off his complaint to commend the plain goods of life as gifts from God: bread, wine, work, friendship, marriage, and the sun on your face. He insists that God has made everything beautiful in its time, even when no one can see the whole. And the book closes with a second voice, a narrator who has been quoting the Teacher all along, who sums up the matter: “Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man” (12:13).

Ecclesiastes matters because it refuses to lie about the world. It names death, injustice, and the way achievement slips through our fingers, and it does so inside Scripture, as part of God's word. Readers who have found easy answers too thin have often found this book honest enough to trust.
author:
The book introduces its speaker as “the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1). The Hebrew title, Qoheleth, is a form of a verb meaning to assemble or gather, so it probably means one who gathers people (a teacher or preacher) or one who gathers sayings. The Greek translation called him Ekklesiastes, a member or leader of an assembly, which gave the book its English name. Jewish and Christian tradition identified the Teacher with Solomon, the son of David famed for wisdom and wealth, and chapters 1 and 2 plainly evoke Solomon's reign.

The book never actually uses Solomon's name, however, and many interpreters, including many conservative ones, think the royal voice is a literary role the author adopts for the first two chapters and then largely sets aside. They point to the Teacher's claim to surpass all who were over Jerusalem before him (1:16), when only David preceded Solomon; to his speaking of kings from the outside in later chapters; and to the Hebrew itself, which is late in style, with features resembling the Hebrew of the Mishnah and with loanwords from Persian such as the word for parks in 2:5. Those who hold to Solomonic authorship answer that the royal claims should be taken at face value and that the language can be explained by the book's genre or later updating. Either way, the book presents itself as the Teacher's words passed on by someone else: a narrator speaks of the Teacher in the third person at 1:1-2, 7:27, and 12:8-14.
date: If Solomon is the author, the book comes from the tenth century BC. Most modern scholars date it much later, in the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BC) or the early Greek period (third century BC), mainly because of its language and its picture of a society of officials, merchants, and absentee rulers. Fragments of Ecclesiastes were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in copies made around the second century BC, which rules out the very latest proposed dates. The question does not change what the book says, and faithful readers hold both positions.
setting:
The book is set, in its own framing, in the court of a king in Jerusalem, and its first two chapters read like the memoir of a monarch who could buy anything. The world it actually describes is broader: a society where people work for wages and profit, where wealth can be lost in a bad venture, where officials watch over officials and the poor are oppressed with no one to comfort them, and where a person's fortune can turn in a day. Whether that world belongs to Solomon's Jerusalem or to Judah under Persian or Greek rule, the first readers were people who knew that hard work does not always pay and that the righteous do not always prosper.

Ecclesiastes belongs to the wisdom tradition of the ancient Near East, alongside Proverbs and Job. Other ancient cultures also produced reflective writings on death and the meaning of toil, and readers have long noticed that the advice to enjoy food, clean clothes, and a beloved wife in 9:7-9 closely resembles counsel given to Gilgamesh by the alewife Siduri in an Old Babylonian version of the Gilgamesh Epic. Ecclesiastes shares these questions but answers them within Israel's faith in one God who made the world and will judge it.
purpose: The book was written to teach wisdom by testing it. It takes the confident patterns of Proverbs (the diligent prosper, the wise are rewarded) and presses them against the hard cases, especially death, which comes to wise and foolish alike. Its aim is to strip away false hopes: that achievement will last, that wisdom can master life, that we can see the whole of God's work. What is left is a humbler and steadier way to live: receiving each day's work and joy as God's gift, fearing God, and leaving the rest to his judgment. The epilogue says the Teacher's words are like goads (12:11), meant to prod and even hurt a little, for the reader's good.
story: Ecclesiastes does not advance the Bible's plot, but it reads like a long meditation on Genesis 3. After Adam's sin the ground is cursed, work becomes toil, and humans return to the dust from which they came, and the Teacher's language of toil, dust, and breath echoes those chapters closely. The same Hebrew consonants as hevel form the name of Abel, the first human to die. The book is set in the reign of David's son, at the height of Israel's glory, and it quietly asks what that glory was worth. In the Hebrew Bible it belongs to the Writings and is one of the five scrolls read at Jewish festivals, traditionally at the Feast of Tabernacles. In Christian Bibles it stands between Proverbs and the Song of Songs.
christ:
The New Testament doesn't quote Ecclesiastes directly, but it takes up its central word. When Paul says in Romans 8 that the creation was subjected to futility in hope, he uses the Greek word that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament used for hevel throughout Ecclesiastes. Paul's point is that the frustration the Teacher describes is real but not final: creation waits to be set free when God's children are revealed.

The Teacher's great problem is death, which erases the difference between the wise and the fool. The New Testament's answer is the resurrection of Jesus, which Paul says means that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Jesus, whom the Gospels call one greater than Solomon, enters the world under the sun, shares its toil and its injustice, and dies. His rising is the new thing the Teacher could not find. This link is thematic, not predictive: Ecclesiastes doesn't foresee Christ, but it names the question to which his resurrection is the Christian answer.
reading:
Read Ecclesiastes as a search, not a list of rulings. The Teacher often reports what he observed and felt at a given point, including conclusions he later qualifies, so a single verse lifted out (for example, that humans have no advantage over animals, 3:19) may not be the book's final word. Watch for the refrains: under the sun, a pursuit of the wind, nothing better than to eat and drink, and the key word hevel.

That word is the heart of the debate. Its basic meaning is vapor or breath. Some translations render it as vanity (the King James tradition) or meaningless (the New International Version), which stress emptiness. Others stress transience, life as a passing breath. Still others read it as enigma or absurdity, what cannot be grasped or made sense of; the scholar Michael V. Fox argued for absurd. The word may carry different shades in different places. Also watch the book's two voices: the Teacher, who speaks in the first person, and the narrator of the frame, whose closing words guide how we hear the rest.

structure.title: Title and opening poem
structure.summary: The narrator introduces the Teacher and his motto, and a poem pictures the endless, wearying cycles of generations, sun, wind, and rivers, where nothing is new and nothing is remembered.

structure.title: The king's experiment
structure.summary: Speaking as a king, the Teacher tests wisdom, pleasure, building, and wealth, and finds that death erases their gains, yet he ends by calling daily food and work a gift from God's hand.

structure.title: A time for everything
structure.summary: The poem of the times, followed by reflection on God's hidden work, eternity in the human heart, injustice, and the shared death of humans and beasts.

structure.title: Observations under the sun
structure.summary: Oppression, envy, loneliness, fickle politics, careful worship, the traps of wealth, and the sorrow of having goods without the power to enjoy them.

structure.title: Wisdom tested
structure.summary: Collections of sayings on what is better, on the limits of wisdom, on living under kings, and on the injustice that no one can explain.

structure.title: Life before death
structure.summary: Since the same end comes to all, the Teacher urges joy, energy, and boldness in the time given, and closes with a haunting poem on old age and death.

structure.title: Epilogue
structure.summary: The narrator repeats the motto, describes the Teacher's work, and gives the conclusion: fear God, keep his commandments, and remember that God will judge every deed.

themes.title: Hevel: breath, vapor, futility
themes.body: The book's key word appears dozens of times and describes the whole of life under the sun. Whether it is best heard as emptiness, brevity, or enigma, it names the experience of grasping at something that won't stay in the hand. The book does not say God's world is worthless; it says that nothing in it can bear the weight of being our ultimate gain.

themes.title: Death, the great leveler
themes.body: The Teacher returns again and again to death, which comes to the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, humans and animals alike. Death exposes the limits of every strategy for securing a legacy. The book forces the reader to face mortality honestly rather than distract from it.

themes.title: Joy as God's gift
themes.body: Seven times the book commends eating, drinking, and finding satisfaction in work, and it calls these the gift of God. This is not despairing hedonism. It is the recognition that ordinary goods, received gratefully day by day, are the portion God gives, even when the larger meaning escapes us.

themes.title: The limits of wisdom
themes.body: Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, and the Teacher never denies it. But wisdom cannot see the whole of God's work, cannot straighten what is crooked, and cannot prevent death. The book teaches humility about what human understanding can achieve.

themes.title: The fear of God and his judgment
themes.body: Beneath the Teacher's questions runs the conviction that God is real, sovereign, and just, even when injustice seems to win. The fitting response is reverent fear, careful worship, and obedience, and the epilogue makes this the book's conclusion: God will bring every deed into judgment.

keyChapters.why: The motto of futility and the poem of endless cycles set the book's question: what does a person gain from all his labor under the sun?
The royal experiment with pleasure, building, and wealth ends in despair over death, then turns to receive food and work as a gift from God's hand.
The famous poem of times and seasons, and the claim that God has set eternity in the human heart.
Counsel on careful worship and vows, and on the emptiness of loving money.
The shared fate of all, followed by the book's warmest call to enjoy life with the people and work God gives.
The poem on old age and death, and the epilogue's conclusion to fear God and keep his commandments.

parts.body:
Ecclesiastes is the twenty-first book of the Bible. It has twelve chapters, and it is the record of a search.

A speaker who calls himself the Teacher, Qoheleth in Hebrew, sets out to find what a person really gains from all the work of a life lived under the sun (1:3). He tests pleasure, great building projects, wealth, wisdom and work. He watches the seasons turn, the powerful crush the weak, the righteous die young and the wicked die honored. Over all of it he sets one word, hevel, which the Berean Standard Bible translates as futility: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” (1:2).

Yet the book is not simply gloomy. Again and again the Teacher breaks off to commend the plain goods of life as gifts from God: bread, wine, work, friendship, marriage, the sun on your face. He says that God ‘has made everything beautiful in its time’ (3:11), even when no one can see the whole. And the book ends with a second voice, a narrator who has been quoting the Teacher all along, who sums up the matter: ‘Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man’ (12:13).

Ecclesiastes refuses to lie about the world. It names death, injustice and the way achievement slips through the fingers, and it does so inside Scripture, as part of God's word. Readers who have found easy answers too thin have often found this book honest enough to trust.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Ecclesiastes belongs to the Bible's wisdom books, with Job and Proverbs. In Christian Bibles it stands between Proverbs and the Song of Songs. In the Hebrew Bible it is one of the Writings, and one of the five short scrolls read at Jewish festivals. It is traditionally read at the Feast of Tabernacles, the autumn harvest festival, where its sober words about the shortness of life sit beside the command to rejoice.

It does not move the Bible's story forward, but it reads like a long meditation on Genesis 3. After the first sin the ground is cursed, work becomes toil, and human beings return to the dust they came from: ‘For dust you are, and to dust you shall return’ (Genesis 3:19). The Teacher's language of toil, dust and breath echoes those chapters closely. The same Hebrew consonants as hevel form the name of Abel, the first human to die.

The book is set in the reign of David's son, at the height of Israel's glory, and it quietly asks what that glory was worth. Proverbs says how life ordinarily goes under God. Ecclesiastes, like Job, presses on the cases where it does not seem to.

The book introduces its speaker as ‘the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem’ (1:1). The Hebrew title, Qoheleth, comes from a verb meaning to gather or assemble, so it probably means one who gathers people, a teacher or preacher, or one who gathers sayings. The Greek translation called him Ekklesiastes, which gave the book its English name.

Jewish and Christian tradition identified the Teacher with Solomon, the son of David famed for wisdom and wealth, and chapters 1 and 2 plainly recall Solomon's reign. Some conservative scholars, such as Duane Garrett, have continued to defend Solomon's authorship, holding that the royal claims should be taken at face value.

But the book never uses Solomon's name, and many interpreters, including many conservative ones, think the royal voice is a literary role the author takes up for the first two chapters and then largely sets aside. They point to the Teacher's claim to surpass all who were over Jerusalem before him (1:16), when only David had reigned there as Israel's king before Solomon. They point to the way he later speaks of kings from the outside. And they point to the Hebrew itself, which is late in style, with loanwords from Persian such as pardes, park (2:5).

So the dates differ widely. If Solomon wrote it, the book comes from the tenth century BC. Most modern scholars place it in the Persian or early Greek period, roughly 450 to 250 BC. Fragments of Ecclesiastes were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in copies made around the second century BC, which rules out the very latest proposals. The question does not change what the book says, and faithful readers hold both positions. These notes take no side.

The book's key word is hevel. It appears thirty-eight times. Its basic meaning is breath or vapor, the mist of breath on a cold morning that is there and then gone.

How to translate it shapes how the whole book is heard. Jerome's Latin rendered it vanitas, which gave the old English translations ‘vanity’. The New International Version has ‘meaningless’. The Berean Standard Bible has ‘futile’ and ‘futility’. Others prefer ‘fleeting’, and the scholar Michael V. Fox argued for ‘absurd’.

These are three different ideas. Emptiness says life is hollow. Brevity says life is a passing breath, not worthless but short. Enigma says life cannot be grasped or figured out. The word may carry different shades in different places.

What the book does not say is that God's world is worthless. It says that nothing under the sun can bear the weight of being a person's final gain. A related refrain runs beside it: ‘a pursuit of the wind’ (1:14), like trying to catch the wind in your hands.

The book has two voices. Most of it is the Teacher speaking in the first person. But a narrator introduces him (1:1-2), steps in once in the middle (7:27), and speaks about him in the third person at the end (12:8-14). The narrator's closing words guide how the rest is heard.

The Teacher's words follow a loose path. A poem pictures the endless cycles of sun, wind and rivers, where nothing is new and nothing is remembered (1:1-11). Then, speaking as a king, the Teacher tests pleasure, building, wealth and wisdom (1:12 to 2:26). Chapter 3 holds the famous poem of times and seasons. Chapters 4 to 6 are observations: oppression, envy, loneliness, careful worship, the traps of money. Chapters 7 and 8 test wisdom itself, with many ‘better than’ sayings. From 9:1 to 12:7, since the same end comes to all, the Teacher urges joy and boldness in the time given, and closes with a haunting poem on old age and death.

Watch for the refrains: under the sun (1:3), a pursuit of the wind (1:14), and the repeated counsel that nothing is better than to eat, drink and find joy in work as God's gift. And watch for the book's opening and closing cry, ‘Futility of futilities’ (1:2; 12:8), which wraps around the whole.

In chapters 1 and 2 the Teacher speaks as a king who can buy anything. He gives himself to wisdom and finds that ‘with much wisdom comes much sorrow’ (1:18). He tries pleasure and laughter. He builds houses, plants vineyards and parks, makes pools, buys servants and herds, gathers silver and gold, and has singers and every delight. He denies himself nothing.

Then he looks at it all: ‘I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun’ (2:11). Wise and foolish die alike and are forgotten alike. Whatever he built will pass to someone who did not work for it, who may be a fool.

His reaction is raw: ‘So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me’ (2:17). The Bible records that cry honestly. It is not counsel. It is the cry of a man who has found that achievement cannot carry the weight he put on it.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The chapter does not end there. It ends with a turn: ‘Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God’ (2:24). The gifts of an ordinary day are not the final gain, but they are real, and they come from God.

Chapter 3 opens with one of the best-known poems in the Bible: ‘To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven’ (3:1). A time to be born and a time to die, to plant and to uproot, to weep and to laugh, to mourn and to dance, to keep silent and to speak, to love and to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. The poem names fourteen pairs, the whole of life from birth to death.

Then the Teacher reflects. People cannot control the times, but God has made everything fitting in its time. ‘He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end’ (3:11). Human beings long for the whole, and cannot see it.

The chapter also faces injustice in the courts, and the hard fact that humans and animals die alike and return to the same dust. ‘Who knows’, the Teacher asks, whether the human spirit goes upward (3:21). He admits what he cannot see. He does not deny what he does not know, and the book later says that ‘the spirit returns to God who gave it’ (12:7).

parts.h: Oppression, and the darkest words in the book
parts.body:
In chapter 4 the Teacher looks at the oppressed and sees ‘the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter’ (4:1). Twice in one verse he says it: no comforter. The power was in the hands of the oppressors.

Then come some of the darkest words in Scripture. He admired the dead above the living, and counted better than both the one who has never been born and so has not seen the evil done under the sun (4:2-3). Some readers take these words as a settled view. Others hear them as the cry of a man overwhelmed by injustice, the kind of cry also heard in Job 3 and Jeremiah 20, where suffering men curse the day they were born. The Bible includes such cries without making them its final word. The book itself moves on: ‘even a live dog is better than a dead lion’ (9:4).

A reader in the dark can find in these verses company, not a verdict. Scripture knows how dark life can look, and makes room for that honesty. It does not say that anyone is better off dead.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The same chapters praise companionship, ‘Two are better than one’ (4:9), counsel careful worship and honest vows (5:1-7), and warn that the love of money never satisfies (5:10).

Chapters 7 and 8 gather sayings, many of them ‘better than’: ‘It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart’ (7:2). Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, and the Teacher never denies it.

But wisdom has limits. It cannot straighten what God has made crooked. It cannot see the whole of God's work. It cannot explain why things go as they do: ‘There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve’ (8:14).

In 7:26-28 the Teacher speaks of a woman who is a snare and says he did not find one upright woman among a thousand. Readers take this in several ways: as the limited observation of a man in his world, which Scripture records without endorsing; as a warning about the seductive woman or Folly of Proverbs 5 to 9, not about women in general; as a comment on Solomon's thousand wives and concubines; or in light of verse 29, which uses the word for all humanity and finds both men and women gone astray. What is clear is that the passage's last word indicts humanity as a whole, and that the rest of Scripture honors women as bearing God's image fully.

parts.h: Eat, drink, and enjoy: the gift of God
parts.body:
Seven times the book commends eating, drinking and finding satisfaction in work, and it calls these the gift of God. This is not careless pleasure-seeking. It is receiving ordinary goods with thanks, day by day, as the portion God gives, even when the larger meaning escapes.

The warmest of these passages is in chapter 9: ‘Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works’ (9:7). Wear white, anoint your head, enjoy life with the wife you love, and ‘Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might’ (9:10).

Readers have long noticed that 9:7-9 closely resembles the counsel given to Gilgamesh by the alewife Siduri in an Old Babylonian version of the Gilgamesh Epic. Ecclesiastes shares the question of what to do with a short life, but it answers within Israel's faith in one God who made the world, who gives these goods, and who will judge it.

The Teacher returns again and again to death, which comes to the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, people and animals. In chapter 9 he says that ‘the dead know nothing’ (9:5) and have no share in what is done under the sun.

Read alone, those verses can sound like a denial of any life after death, and some groups have used them that way. Several things help. The Teacher speaks deliberately of life under the sun, the world as seen from inside human experience. He describes the absence of the dead from this world, not a full account of their state. The Old Testament's light on life beyond death grows over time, with clear words of resurrection coming later (Daniel 12:2). And the Teacher himself says that the spirit returns to God (12:7) and that God will bring every deed into judgment (12:14), which assumes something beyond the grave.

The book's last poem (12:1-7) pictures old age and death as a great house falling silent: the keepers tremble, the grinders stop, the windows grow dim, the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl broken, and ‘the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it’ (12:7). It is told with dignity, and it is prefaced with a plea: ‘Remember your Creator in the days of your youth’ (12:1).

parts.h: The Teacher's voice, and the epilogue
parts.body:
The book ends with the narrator. He says the Teacher was wise, taught the people, and arranged many proverbs, and that the words of the wise are like goads, sharp sticks that prod an ox along (12:9-11). Then he gives the conclusion: ‘Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil’ (12:13-14).

Readers have heard the relation between the Teacher and this ending in very different ways. Some, such as James Crenshaw in his 1987 commentary, take the Teacher as a skeptic whose view of God is dark and distant, with the ending added later to make the book acceptable. R. N. Whybray, in a 1982 article, called the Teacher a preacher of joy, stressing the repeated call to enjoy life as God's gift. Building on Michael Fox's work on the frame narrator, Tremper Longman, in his 1998 commentary, and others read the body of the book as the words of a searching, unsettled Teacher whom the narrator presents and then weighs, so that the final word is the narrator's. Derek Kidner, in The Message of Ecclesiastes (1976), and many preachers read the Teacher as deliberately exploring life ‘under the sun’, without the light of revelation, to show that such a life cannot satisfy.

Some note that the fear of God and his judgment are not new in the epilogue: the Teacher himself commanded the fear of God (5:7) and warned of judgment (3:17; 11:9). On that reading the ending does not overturn the search. It names where the search was heading. The question of how the book was put together is open, and these notes take no side. Readers across these views agree that the book as it stands asks to be read with its conclusion.

parts.h: A book the rabbis argued over
parts.body:
The book's place in Scripture was itself debated. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records rabbinic disagreement about whether Ecclesiastes defiles the hands, the rabbis' way of saying a book is holy Scripture. The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) records that the sages wished to withdraw it because it seems to contradict itself, but kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah.

Its place was kept, and its lines have entered common speech, from nothing new under the sun to a time to be born and a time to die. Its third chapter has been set to music many times.

That the book was argued over is part of its gift. It is Scripture that argues, that doubts out loud, and that still ends in the fear of God.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Ecclesiastes
parts.body:
The New Testament does not quote Ecclesiastes directly, but it takes up its central word. When Paul writes that ‘the creation was subjected to futility’ (Romans 8:20), he uses the Greek word that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament used for hevel throughout Ecclesiastes. And he says that it was subjected ‘in hope’, waiting to be ‘set free from its bondage to decay’ (Romans 8:20-21). The frustration the Teacher describes is real, but it is not final.

The Teacher's great problem is death, which wipes out the difference between the wise and the fool. The New Testament's answer is the resurrection of Jesus, which is why Paul can say that ‘your labor in the Lord is not in vain’ (1 Corinthians 15:58). That link is thematic, not predictive. Ecclesiastes does not foresee Christ. It names the question to which, in Christian faith, his resurrection is the answer.

These notes keep to the lines the New Testament and the site's book page draw, and add no others.

Read Ecclesiastes as a search, not a list of rulings. The Teacher often reports what he saw and felt at one point, including conclusions he later qualifies. A single verse lifted out, such as the claim that people have no advantage over animals (3:19), may not be the book's final word.

Read it whole, and watch where the narrator speaks (1:1-2; 7:27; 12:8-14). Watch for the refrains: under the sun, a pursuit of the wind, nothing better than to eat and drink, and hevel.

Let it be honest with you. It does not hurry anyone out of grief or pretend that injustice makes sense. It gives words to the dark, and then it gives the plain gifts of a day, bread, work, friendship and love, as things to receive from God's hand.

And read it beside Job and Proverbs. Proverbs says how life usually goes. Job and Ecclesiastes say what happens when it does not. All three end in the same place: the fear of God.

hard.line: Futility of futilities. Hevel means breath or vapor; readers hear emptiness, brevity or enigma. Nothing under the sun can be a person's final gain.
With much wisdom comes much sorrow. Knowing more does not make life lighter, and the Teacher says so.
‘So I hated life’. The cry of a man whose achievements could not carry his hopes, recorded honestly, never as counsel.
Eat, drink and enjoy your work: not careless pleasure, but ordinary gifts received from God's hand.
People and animals share one fate. The Teacher asks who knows, admitting what he cannot see; 12:7 says the spirit returns to God.
The dead better off than the living. A cry like Job 3 and Jeremiah 20, not the book's final word (9:4), and never a verdict on anyone's life.
Do not be surprised at oppression: a realistic word about layers of officials, not an approval of injustice.
A man with everything who never enjoys it, set beside a stillborn child who has rest: a cry about joyless years, not a judgment on any child or parent.
Do not be overly righteous, nor overly wicked (7:16-17), with verse 20: no one is righteous without sin. Not a call to moderate sin.
Not one upright woman in a thousand. Read several ways; its last word indicts all humanity, and Scripture honors women fully.
The righteous get what the wicked deserve. The book admits what Proverbs' patterns cannot explain.
The dead know nothing: their absence from life under the sun, not the book's full account (12:7, 14).
Eat your bread with joy: close to Siduri's counsel in Gilgamesh, but given within faith in the God who gives and judges.
Money answers everything: an observation, perhaps ironic, about what money can buy, not a creed.
Walk in the ways of your heart: joy commended, held together with God's judgment in the same verse.
The epilogue: part of the design or a later addition, and the narrator's stance toward the Teacher, read several ways.

words.line: Breath or vapor, the book's key word, thirty-eight times: futility, vanity, meaninglessness, fleeting, enigma (1:2).
The Teacher: one who gathers people or gathers sayings. Greek Ekklesiastes gave the book its name (1:1).
Gain, advantage or profit, a word found in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes. What does a man gain? (1:3)
A pursuit of the wind: chasing what cannot be caught. A refrain beside hevel (1:14).
Toil or labor, often with a sense of trouble or weariness, the work done under the sun (2:18).
What happens, fate or a chance event, above all death, which comes to wise and fool alike (2:14; 9:2).
Park or garden, a loanword from Persian, the word behind the English ‘paradise’ (2:5).
Joy or pleasure: tested and found wanting as a final gain (2:1), and commended as God's gift (8:15).
Time or season: a time for everything under heaven, fourteen pairs from birth to death (3:1-8).
A long duration, eternity. God has set eternity in human hearts, though they cannot fathom his work (3:11).
Portion or lot: the share of life, food, work and love God gives, to be received with joy (5:18; 9:9).
To fear or revere. The fear of God runs through the book (5:7) and is its conclusion (12:13).
Good or better: the many ‘better than’ sayings that weigh one thing against another (7:1-10).
The realm of the dead, where there is no work or planning or knowledge (9:10).
Goad, the pointed stick that prods an ox. The words of the wise are like goads (12:11).

timeline.what: Solomon reigns in Jerusalem, famed for wisdom, wealth and building. The Teacher of chapters 1 and 2 speaks in his voice.

timeline.when: The tenth century BC, on one view
timeline.what: If Solomon wrote the book, as Jewish and Christian tradition held and some conservative scholars still argue, it comes from his reign.

timeline.when: About 450 to 250 BC, on another view
timeline.what: Most modern scholars place the book in the Persian or early Greek period, mainly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords.
Copies of Ecclesiastes are made that were later found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, ruling out the very latest proposed dates.
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, saying that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).
Paul writes Romans and says the creation was subjected to futility in hope, using the Greek word for hevel (Romans 8:20-21).
Derek Kidner publishes The Message of Ecclesiastes, reading the Teacher as exploring life under the sun without revelation.
R. N. Whybray calls the Teacher a preacher of joy.
James Crenshaw's commentary reads the Teacher as a skeptic, with the ending added to make the book acceptable.
Tremper Longman's commentary reads the narrator as presenting the Teacher and then weighing him.
